responseText: {"galleries":[{"id":"nnotb--settings-and-light","title":"Ground, Light, Surround","question":"When does the space around a subject carry as much visual weight as the subject itself?","introduction":"Sixteen works move between open landscape and enclosed figure, between cast light and dense mark. None of them lets the background stay neutral. A building dissolves into its field; a face is split across two color zones; a valley holds as much visual weight as any portrait. Five chapters trace how surrounding space can redirect, contain, or reframe what sits inside it.","closing":"Each work leaves the boundary between subject and surround unsettled. Whether that instability comes from light, ground, or enclosing geometry remains an open question across every room.","chapters":[{"title":"Grounds That Will Not Recede","introduction":"Three works where the space beneath and around a form is as visually active as anything placed on it — the ground competes rather than supports."},{"title":"Canopy, Cloud, Open Air","introduction":"Three works where marks accumulate into something sky-like or foliage-like, and the boundary between inside and outside becomes genuinely uncertain."},{"title":"Faces and Fields","introduction":"Four works where a face is surrounded by color zones or enclosing marks that divide or reframe it, plus one abstract field showing what remains when the face is absent."},{"title":"Light as Enclosure","introduction":"Four works where light does not simply illuminate but surrounds or structures the forms inside it, making the lit space feel sealed rather than open."},{"title":"Geometry and Scatter","introduction":"Three works where surrounding space is organized by bars, arches, and zigzag lines that hold or release the forms sitting inside them."}]},{"id":"nnotb--letters-and-signs","title":"Letters Among the Marks","question":"When a readable word appears inside a painted surface, does it direct looking or compete with it?","introduction":"Across fourteen works, words and symbols appear on the same surface as faces, figures, and dense mark-making. Sometimes a word names what we see; sometimes it sits inside a body or floats as pure shape. Five chapters trace what happens at that boundary — where reading and looking pull in different directions, and neither fully resolves the other.","closing":"Each work places a legible sign inside a field that resists easy reading. Whether the word clarifies or complicates what surrounds it is a question each work answers differently.","chapters":[{"title":"The Word Inside the Body","introduction":"Three works carry explicit text absorbed into or standing apart from a figure, treating language as a material element rather than a caption or title."},{"title":"Signs That Behave as Shapes","introduction":"Three works carry marks that resemble writing or symbols but resist full decoding, functioning as visual weight and rhythm rather than readable content."},{"title":"Faces Without Anchors","introduction":"Three works build faces from glowing voids, scribbled masses, and competing color zones — present as figures but without the stability a readable sign might provide."},{"title":"Text as Costume and Label","introduction":"Two works place legible text on or near figures as a worn or projected identity, where the word becomes a prop or badge rather than a description."},{"title":"Everything at Once","introduction":"Two works push marks, motifs, text, and assembled parts to every edge simultaneously, testing how much a single surface holds before any hierarchy collapses."}]},{"id":"nnotb--radiating-lines","title":"Lines Moving Outward","question":"When marks spread away from a central form, what changes as that center becomes more complex or begins to dissolve?","introduction":"Seventeen works share one structural habit: lines, waves, zigzags, or spikes move outward from a central form. What those marks carry shifts constantly — from stillness to agitation, from tight order to dispersal. Four chapters follow that spread, tracking what changes when the radiating mark is sparse or dense, and when the center itself starts to break apart.","closing":"Each work sends marks outward from something. How those marks read depends on what the center looks like — and how much of it remains visible.","chapters":[{"title":"Still Centers, Spreading Lines","introduction":"Three works open with the simplest version: a single dark figure on a flat field, lines fanning outward with almost no competing marks elsewhere on the surface."},{"title":"The Figure Gains a Face","introduction":"Four works add facial features — eyes, mouths, spiral marks — to the radiating silhouette, asking whether a legible face changes how the surrounding lines read."},{"title":"Faces That Fill the Frame","introduction":"Four works expand the face until it crowds the available space, and the radiating marks become inseparable from the surface rather than separate from the figure."},{"title":"When the Center Loosens","introduction":"Five works close the exhibition by complicating or dispersing the center through layered spirals, curtained enclosures, and surfaces where radiating mark and ground become indistinguishable."}]}]}
